title: Analysis of the Pass-ta-key Attack on Passkeys: Clarifying Misconceptions
summary: The article clarifies misconceptions about the Pass-ta-key attack, which exploits malware on Windows to extract passkeys from Google Password Manager. It explains that passkeys are not universally stored in hardware-based secure enclaves (e.g., TPMs) due to syncing limitations, and that Windows' weaker app sandboxing makes it more vulnerable to such attacks compared to other platforms. The attack is not novel but highlights inherent risks when malware compromises a device logged into sensitive accounts.
key_points: Pass-ta-key is an attack that extracts passkeys from Google Password Manager on Windows when the device is infected with malware.
Contrary to common belief, passkeys are not universally stored in hardware-based secure enclaves (e.g., TPMs, secure enclaves) due to syncing limitations across devices.
Most platforms (macOS, iOS, Android) store passkeys locally, while Windows often relies on cloud-based end-to-end encrypted storage (e.g., Google Password Manager, 1Password).
Windows' weaker app sandboxing allows malware to access data from other apps, unlike stricter sandboxing on other platforms.
The attack is not novel; it exploits the inherent risk of malware on a compromised device logged into sensitive accounts.
Passkeys eliminate shared secrets (e.g., passwords) but are not designed to withstand physical attacks or malware on the device storing them.
The research underscores the importance of device security, especially on Windows, where malware can more easily access sensitive data.
